title: Choosing the safest water source
summary: Which water to take first, from stored water and drilled wells down to beaver ponds, and what each usually carries; what to look for upstream; why spring melt, beaver dams and wildfires make water worse. Everything except stored water you trust needs treating, and boiling and bleach deal with germs, not fuel, salt, metals or most chemicals, so picking the source is your main defence against those.

steps.text: Before you fill anything, walk or look upstream, and up the slope from a well or spring. Note houses and septic fields, barns and manure, roads and salt piles, dumps, fuel tanks, mines and burned buildings (Ottawa threats, USGS mine drainage).

Collect above the highest of those, or choose another source. Take the least exposed source you can reach: stored water you trust, then a drilled well, then a spring or rain, then a stream, then a pond. That is a rough order of exposure, not a safety grade: the WHO/UNICEF ladder only sorts sources into improved, unimproved and surface water (JMP ladder), and water from outside the home must be treated whatever the source (CDC find water).
Skip water with floating material, a dark colour or an odd smell (EPA 2017), and anything that fuel may have reached (CDC find water) or that has a bloom.
steps.warn: Water that fuel or toxic chemicals may have reached can't be made safe by boiling or disinfecting, and shouldn't be used for drinking or bathing (CDC emergency, CDC find water). Blooms: boiling doesn't remove their toxins and can raise them; see the blue-green algae card.

steps.text: In spring melt and after heavy rain, expect more germs, manure and road salt in surface water and shallow wells. Use stored or deep-well water if you can (NL Well Aware, Alberta Ag parasites, UTRCA road salt).

After a wildfire, divert the first rain off any ash-covered roof (NSW Health bushfire), and don't drink or cook with tap or well water from a burned area until it has been tested (Purdue wildfire wells for wells, EPA wildfire VOCs for taps).
steps.warn: Don't boil water that may hold benzene or other fire chemicals, or use it hot in a shower: boiling or hot use could put the chemicals in the air you breathe (EPA wildfire VOCs).

steps.text: Treat everything from outside the home (wells, springs, rain, snow, streams, ponds) and any stored water you can't vouch for: clear it first, then disinfect (CDC find water, EPA 2017). For stream, pond and beaver-pond water, boil it, or filter it with a cyst-rated filter and then add chlorine for viruses (see [Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters)). Chlorine alone is weak against Giardia and Cryptosporidium, and most portable filters don't stop viruses (HealthLinkBC 10, WHO TN5, CDC hiking).

notes:
## The ladder, least exposed first
The WHO and UNICEF sort drinking water sources by how they are built and protected. **Improved** sources can deliver safe water because of how they are built: piped water, drilled wells (boreholes), protected dug wells, protected springs, rainwater, and bottled or delivered water. **Unimproved** means an unprotected dug well or spring. **Surface water** (river, lake, pond, stream, canal, dam) is the bottom rung (JMP ladder). Improved only means it *can* be safe. After a disaster any of them can be contaminated, and water from outside the home must be treated to kill germs (CDC find water). The ladder stops at those three groups; the order of the rows below is a rough guide to how exposed each source is, not a safety grade, and none is safe to drink untreated except stored water you trust.

| Source | What it usually carries | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Stored water you trust: sealed bottles, the tap side of the water heater, ice made from clean water, a clear toilet tank with no cleaner in it | Whatever the supply had when it was stored | Pool and spa water is for washing, not drinking. Never the home heating system's tank (CDC find water). See [Water in a building](#guides/reference_building_water). |
| Drilled well, cased and capped | Least exposed of the wells. Bacteria after floods and heavy rain; nitrate near farms and septic fields (HC well test) | Test for bacteria every 6 months, best in early spring, autumn and after heavy rain or floods (HC well test). |
| Protected spring | Groundwater close to the surface, so more open to contamination than a typical well (Penn State springs) | In tests of 37 Pennsylvania roadside springs, 91% failed at least one drinking standard and E. coli and sediment were above limits in over 30%. In follow-up sampling in 2014 to 2015 of a smaller set of the springs, 88% held Giardia or Cryptosporidium at one or both sample times, usually at low levels (Penn State springs). CDC lists natural springs among the outside sources that must be treated (CDC find water). |
| Rain from a clean roof | Dust, smoke and bird droppings; lead, copper or asbestos from roofing, gutters and pipes. The first flow off the roof carries the most dirt, germs and chemicals (CDC rainwater) | CDC: rainwater is not necessarily safe to drink without first removing germs and chemicals (CDC rainwater). See [Rainwater collection](#guides/build_rainwater_collection). |
| Dug or shallow well | Wells under 6 m (20 ft) are at higher risk than drilled ones because the water table is close to the surface (NL Well Aware) | Snowmelt and runoff carry surface dirt into them (NL Well Aware). |
| Snow | Depends where it lay. Stored snow from roads and lots can carry chloride, sodium and petroleum hydrocarbons (Ottawa threats) | See [Water from snow](#guides/skill_water_from_snow). |
| River, stream, lake | Most surface water in Canada has some Giardia and Cryptosporidium (HC protozoa) | Flowing water is generally better than still, but EPA says to treat it whatever the source (EPA 2017). Through ice: read [Water through the ice](#guides/skill_water_through_ice) and the [cold water card](#browse/hazards/cold_water) first. |
| Pond, beaver pond, ditch, floodwater | Beaver dams may hold back parasites washed down from the watershed above (Alberta Ag parasites); runoff from everything around it | Last resort. Skip any with a bloom (below). |

**Walk away from:** water with floating material, a dark colour or an odd smell (EPA 2017), and any water that fuel or toxic chemicals may have reached. CDC says that water cannot be made safe, for drinking or for bathing, and boiling or disinfecting doesn't fix it (CDC find water, CDC emergency). Water that has run past a mine, landfill, dump or chemical store may carry metals, salts or chemicals, and boiling and chlorine don't remove those (EPA water, USGS mine drainage, Ottawa threats): pick another source. The home heating system's tank is never drinking water (CDC find water).

## Upstream of what
Ontario's Clean Water Act, 2006 names 21 prescribed threats to municipal wells and water intakes, and the City of Ottawa's summary lists them (Ottawa threats). They make a handy checklist for what to look for upstream of where you fill, and on the slope above a well or spring:
- **Waste:** landfills, dumps, stored waste oil and hazardous waste, septage spread on fields.
- **Sewage:** septic systems, sewers, sewage plants, stormwater ponds.
- **Farms:** pasture, barnyards and outdoor livestock pens; manure, sewage biosolids and food-processing waste spread on land; fertiliser and pesticides (golf courses too).
- **Roads:** road salt where it is spread and where it is stored; snow dumps (chloride, sodium, petroleum hydrocarbons).
- **Fuel:** bulk plants, gas stations, cardlocks, marinas, farm and contractor yards, home heating oil tanks.
- **Solvents:** dry cleaners and anywhere paint, degreasers and glues are stored.
- **Airports:** glycol de-icing runoff.

Mine tunnels that drain into streams add metals and acid to them (USGS mine drainage). CAWST's rules for protecting a source: latrines downhill and at least 30 m from it, animals fenced away, and washing and animal watering kept downstream of where people collect (CAWST factsheets). Many of these threats are invisible from the bank, so read the map and the land, not just the water.

## Spring melt, heavy rain and road salt
The worst water of the year comes with the thaw:
- Melting snow and running water carry surface contaminants into wells, which is why early spring and the day after heavy rain are good times to test (NL Well Aware, HC well test).
- In an Alberta study of the North Saskatchewan basin, the risk of Giardia and Cryptosporidium in drinking water was highest during spring runoff and heavy rain, streams draining farmland carried the most parasites, and spring levels tracked livestock numbers and cattle yards along the streams (Alberta Ag parasites).
- Meltwater and runoff carry road salt's chloride into streams, rivers and groundwater, and it builds up over time (UTRCA road salt). Keep salty snow piles away from wells and ditches (UTRCA road salt). Boiling and bleach don't remove salts (EPA water).

If you have a choice in spring, use stored water or a deep well over surface water, and take surface water upstream of roads and fields.

## Beaver ponds and Giardia
Giardiasis is sometimes called "beaver fever" (HealthLinkBC 10). Giardia cysts survive in lakes, ponds, creeks and streams (HealthLinkBC 10), including in cold water, and get there from human and animal droppings in or near the water (BCCDC giardiasis). In an Alberta study, beaver and muskrat droppings held a lot of Giardia and the authors judged it likely that they add to stream Giardia, but they found no link between beaver activity along the streams and parasite levels. Dams may hold back parasites washed down from the watershed above them, and breached dams likely added to high parasite levels in non-farm streams during summer runoff (Alberta Ag parasites). Cysts survive in cold water, so don't count on cold or ice to make a pond safer.

What works on Giardia:
- **Boiling:** a rolling boil for at least 1 minute (HealthLinkBC 10). Above 2,000 m, 2 minutes (BCCDC giardiasis).
- **A filter** with an absolute pore size of 1 micron or less, or an NSF rating for cyst removal. Jug filters such as Brita don't remove it (BCCDC giardiasis). Most portable filters remove parasites but not viruses (CDC hiking), so where sewage may be upstream, boil, or chlorinate after filtering. See [Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters) and [Test a water filter](#guides/test_water_filter).
- **Chlorine is weak on it.** BC's health services call Giardia moderately resistant and chlorine generally not effective (HealthLinkBC 10), and Health Canada expects Giardia and Cryptosporidium to survive normal chlorine residuals (Health Canada chlorine TD). Cryptosporidium is no different: WHO says it resists chlorine, and CDC says chlorine tablets won't kill it (WHO TN5, CDC emergency). So boil beaver-pond water, or filter it with a cyst-rated filter and chlorinate afterwards for viruses.

## Blue-green algae
Scum, paint-like streaks or pea-soup water may hold toxins. Boiling doesn't remove them and can even raise their concentration (HealthLinkBC 47); normal bleach doses and most home filters don't reliably remove them either (see the card). Blooms can keep growing under snow and ice, and the toxins can stay in the water long after a bloom has gone (HealthLinkBC 47). Treat any bloom as toxic, don't drink, cook with or bathe in the water, and use another source: read the [blue-green algae card](#browse/hazards/cyanobacteria).

## After a wildfire
**Rain off a burned or ash-covered roof.** NSW Health (Australia) says rainwater from a fire-hit roof may carry ash, debris, dead birds or animals and fire retardant. It calls ash and debris unlikely to be a health risk and the retardants used in Australia low in toxicity, but they spoil the look and taste. Disconnect the downpipes and let the first rain after the fire run to waste unless the roof has been cleaned, and clean it only if that can be done safely. Water that tastes, looks or smells odd, or comes from a burnt tank, liner or pipes, isn't for drinking (NSW Health bushfire). Don't climb into a burnt tank to clean it: NSW Health says working inside a tank can be very dangerous (NSW Health bushfire).

**Tap and well water in a burned area.** After the 2017 and 2018 California wildfires, benzene and other volatile organic compounds (VOCs) were found in water mains, service lines and building fixtures (EPA wildfire VOCs). Two causes are proposed: PVC, HDPE and other plastic pipe, valves and meters breaking down in the heat, and smoke and hot gases sucked into the lines when pressure dropped. VOCs can soak into some plastics, such as polyethylene, and into rubber, and leak back out slowly, and pipes can be contaminated with no visible damage (EPA wildfire VOCs). EPA says boiling such water, or running it hot in a shower, could put the chemicals in the air you breathe until contamination is ruled out (EPA wildfire VOCs).

For a private well after a fire, Purdue's plumbing safety centre lists signs of trouble: lost pressure, discoloured water, heat damage, broken or leaking pipes and tanks, melted plastic parts, ash or debris near or in the system. Use another source until testing shows the water is safe (Purdue wildfire wells). Alberta's advice on returning home: check the well or cistern and test before using it, and run all cold taps for at least 5 minutes (AHS wildfire water). EPA says the only way to find out whether water holds VOCs is to send samples for analysis (EPA wildfire VOCs); see [Test water with found kits](#guides/test_water) for what home kits do cover. With no lab, don't drink, cook with or heat tap or well water from a burned area; use stored water or a source outside the burn.

## What treatment can and can't fix
WHO's emergency note says the household methods it covers (settling, filtering, boiling, chlorine) remove dirt and germs, not chemical contamination, that settled water still needs disinfecting, and that Cryptosporidium resists chlorine (WHO TN5). Boiling or bleach won't remove heavy metals, salts or most chemicals (EPA water). So choosing the source is your main defence against fuel, solvents, pesticides, salt and metals: choose it well, then [clear cloudy water](#guides/skill_settle_with_alum) and disinfect it ([Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters), [Test water with found kits](#guides/test_water)).
